Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege in connection with a story which appeared in yesterday's Ottawa Evening Journal about the fate of certain questions asked by myself. A direct quotation was included in the story. It has been my experience that one who makes a statement is as the mother; the reporter is very often in the place of the father, and the child always takes after the father. The words attributed to me in the story are:
"I'm having a lot of questions turned down these days," he complained, "and I am getting mad about it."
The inference unfortunately is that we are not getting the service we expect from the officials of the house. I should like to dispel that inference immediately. I have nothing but praise for the cooperation and assistance which we do get. Whatever slighting reference there is in the story applies entirely to the government.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: TRUCE IN STRIKE IN UNITED STATES-DELIVERIES TO CANADA
speechtext: May I direct a question to the Minister of Reconstruction, notice of which I have already given him? What steps, if any, has the Minister of Reconstruction taken to assure the delivery to Canada of a fair proportion of the coal that will be mined in the United States during the two weeks of truce in the coal strike?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction) :
maintopic: TRUCE IN STRIKE IN UNITED STATES-DELIVERIES TO CANADA
speechtext: In reply to the hon. member I may say that the solid fuels administration has issued orders restricting the delivery of the coal mined during the truce period to certain classes of essential users whose stock position is such as to require immediate delivery. The same classes of consumers in Canada, whose stocks are below the minimum will, I understand, receive the same treatment as those in the United States. Beyond this, I would point out that coal from the mines must first be supplied to United States railways whose services are vital if the coal is to continue to move at all.
On the orders of the day:

I did not send the minister notice of the question I am going to ask about Drumheller coal. I know he is a walking encyclopsedia on the coal question and does not need notice. My question is: What is the present situation in connection with Drumheller coal production, and is it likely that a substantial tonnage of Drumheller coal will be shipped to Ontario for next winter's requirements?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction) :
speechtext: The production in the Alberta fields is satisfactory. Each succeeding month is higher than the preceding month. It would seem that the area is producing all the coal that the available man-power will permit. The coal controller is moving as much of the coal east as he believes can be spared from this area. There will be a considerable amount of Alberta coal in Ontario this year. Steps are being taken to give incentive to increase the production of all the coal mined in Canada, and it is hoped that production, over and above the normal amount, will contribute to easing the serious situation which is facing us.
Would the minister say whether or not we are receiving Welsh coal at the present time?
No Welsh coal is coming into Canada at the present time. I am sure the hon. member knows that the United Kingdom itself is short of coal.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext:
I was saying a few words on this section when the committee adjourned last night. I wish to continue my remarks, but before going on to deal with the peculiar confusion that seems to exist among the members to my immediate right, where one section is urging that the government give up legislating by order in council and another section is urging that the government continue with it, I want to make reference to a statement made last night by the hon. member for New Westminster. Speaking on this section the hon. member said, as reported at page 1486 of Hansard:
Supposedly the new law did not impose compulsion, but every Japanese family that I knew of registered their children with the Japanese consul. When these people appeared before the committee of this house which sat in 1935 and again in 1936 they were asked to which country they owed allegiance. This was long before there was any question of racial hatred or thought of war. They said without hesitation that they were citizens of Japan.
A number of wild statements of that kind have been made and I think the best thing I can do is to answer the hon. member for New Westminster by quoting a statement made in the committee on the elections and franchise acts which sat in 1936 and 1937, and not in 1935 and 1936. The hon. member for Davenport was questioning one of the witnesses who appeared before the committee, and I quote from the procedings as follows:
Mr. MacNicol: You are Canadian born?
Professor Hayakawa:	I might tell you, for
the information of Mr. Reid, who seems to question our loyalty-
Mr. Reid:	No; hold on a minute. Just get
away from that. I have never questioned your loyalty nor do I. The inference I was drawing is that Japan has the first claim, because your children are registered in Japan, in time of trouble.
Professor Hayakawa:	No; Canada has the
first claim because we are here.
Surely if we feel that our case is just, we should not use material in support except what can be vouched for. The same question arises with regard to the 1,600 Japanese-Cana-dians who are supposed to have gone from Canada to Japan and to have fought against Canada in the Japanese army. May I say here and now that there is no definite evidence on that that anyone can bring forward in this committee.
I should like now to continue with the point I raised last night as to the different points of view in the official opposition in connection with orders in council. First I should like to quote what was said by the hon. member for Lake Centre, as reported on page 513 of Hansard of April 2. I believe the hon. member was acting as the chief spokesman for the official opposition on that occasion, because he followed the Secretary of State in the debate on the motion for second reading of this bill. Referring to the orders in council, which I mentioned last night, he said:
The order in council P.C. 6577, and the order in council of October 5, 1945, P.C. 6444, which I believe will always be remembered as the forgotten order in council, interfere with the fundamental rights of citizenship which were referred to by the Secretary of State. Is it not time that in this country as in Great Britain these rights shall not be interfered with except under a law passed by the parliament of Canada?
I agree with that absolutely, and I suppose when the hon. member for Lake Centre made that statement he made it without reference to race, creed or colour. As I said before, having spoken in the debate immediately after the Secretary of State who introduced the bill I imagine he was speaking as the leading speaker for the official opposition. But what are we to say, what are we to think, when we pick up Hansard of April 5 and read what the hon. member for Vancouver South had to say? This is another prominent member of the official opposition, and at page 619 he said:
We intend to hold the government to its policy. We ask also that the whole of British Columbia he made a protective zone permanently as a defence measure. That is the policy advocated by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie). I hope he has not changed his mind since the announcement he made just a little over a year ago.
Canadian Citizenship

And then again, in the next column:
Parliament can empower the government to act on this question. We will support the government. I am confident that the Social Credit party will support them because of the stand they have taken throughout. The C.C.F. will not.
What I want to ask is this: What policy was the hon. member for Vancouver South insisting that the government should carry out? The policy of deportation, the policy of revoking naturalization and deporting Canadian citizens? Are we not entitled to ask who is speaking for the official opposition? Is it the hon. member for Lake Centre or the hon. member for Vancouver South, or does the official opposition speak with two voices?
In the second paragraph from which I read, the hon. member for Vancouver South said that "parliament can empower the government to act on this question". "We will support the government." That is: "We will support the government" if it brings to this house a bill to revoke the naturalization of Canadian citizens, to make non-citizens. of people who were born in Canada. Then the hon. member generously included hon. members of the Social Credit party to my left. When the hon. member makes this statement in support of a bill he wishes the government to bring in, is he speaking for the hon. member for Lake Centre? Is he speaking for the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario? Is he speaking for the hon. member for Calgary West? Yes, is he speaking for any number of hon. members in the opposition, whose names I could mention, who have expressed themselves as astounded and perturbed by the policy of the government under which, by order in council, it takes away the rights of citizens? That is something this committee is entitled to know.
I too suggest to the government that they bring in a bill of this kind. When parliament refused to accept the emergency powers bill, and insisted upon a completely revised bill, the government reluctantly complied. In my opinion the government had no right to issue the orders in council. It should have had the courage to come to this house and ask parliament for permission to do what it wanted to do. Then we would have found out who stands for liberty-liberty without regard to race, colour, creed or language, or just liberty for the chosen few.
Later on in his speech of April 5 the hon. member for Vancouver South labelled as "pressure groups" those who have been working in all parts of Canada to prevent the government doing this iniquitous thing. The hon. member referred to the editor of Saturday Night, the editor of the Winnipeg Free Press,

and the editor of the Toronto Star. But I noticed there were omissions in his list of "pressure groups," including, at least one other editor who has supported the hon. member in his elections, but who does not support him on this issue. I refer to the Vancouver Daily Province. There were certain other pressure groups to which he did not refer. Among these can be found the Church of England in Canada, and the United Church of Canada, of which he is a member. He did not refer to either of these. Nor did he refer to the National Council of Women, to the Young Women's Christian Association, or to dozens of other "pressure groups." Pressure groups indeed! Anyone is a "pressure group" who will interfere with those who want to destroy liberty. They had pressure groups in Germany. They were the decent people of Germany. Hitler put them into the concentration camps.
Let us see what the Vancouver Daily Province has to say in its editorial of February 21, 1946, where it makes reference to the judgment of the supreme court. Before I read, let me remind hon. members, if they do not already know it, that the Vancouver Daily Province is the leading daily paper in British Columbia. It states:
The judgment of the supreme court on Japanese deportation touches the lives and destinies of 10,000 to 15,000 people of Japanese blood and may have tragic consequences for every one of them. But that is not all it does.
It also touches the lives and destinies of 12,000,000 Canadians, and the consequences to them may be tragic, too, if they do not take steps to protect themselves. The judgment is thus of greater importance to the Canadians who will remain at home than to the Japanese and the Japanese Canadians who may be deported under it.
And farther down:
The real question, however, is not what the government may or may not do.' The question is what it has the power to do. No government, it is not too much to say, should have the power to deport any Canadian citizen and no parliament should have the power to confer such authority upon a government.
In the last election the Vancouver Province did not support me; but it supports, and supports nobly, the policy I espouse on this question. The editorial continues:
There are certain rights which' are vital and fundamental. They should not be subject to revocation or destruction or interference. They should be sacred. Citizenship is one of these rights. The people of the United States, long ago, saw to it that their fundamental rights were safe-guarded. They placed a bill of rights in their constitution, and no president, no state or federal administration, no congress or court can interfere with them

Canadian Citizenship
And concluding:
Seven hundred thousand Canadians fought recently to protect fundamental rights. Tens of thousands laid down their lives. Are we going, now, to allow these fundamental rights to go bydefault? Or are we going to do something to guarantee them?
It is for those reasons that with the member for Vancouver South I would like to see the government bring into this house a bill to empower it to do what it did m an underhand way. At the very time we were discussing the emergency powers transition bill this government was drafting orders in council to put into effect what parliament said should not go into effect.
I do not think the hon. member for Vancouver South was really speaking for British Columbia. I have in my hand a clipping from the Vancouver News-Herald of March 23, 1946. It is J. K. Nesbitt's column, "Day in the House". It deals with the doings of the legislature during the session in Victoria. The subheading is "Putnam Wants Japs to Stay". Mr. Putnam is the minister of agriculture in British Columbia.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext: And a good man.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext:
A good man, I have not the slightest doubt. I believe he is a good man, and I think I shall prove it. I quote now:
Mr. Putnam was the first M.L.A. this session to refer to Japs. Time was when mention of this unfortunate section of Canadian people was sure to stir up a storm. The minister expressed concern that the Japs might be removed from the Okanagan. If this happens, said Mr. Putnam, it will be tough for the farmer, who desperately needs help.
Mr. Nesbitt concludes the paragraph:
Quite a change from the days when we heard Japanese-Canadians were useless.
I have one more quotation to make from the Vancouver Province, and I quote it because of all the indignities which have been heaped one after the other on the Japanese-Canadians. We have had Japanese in British Columbia for a long time. They fought in the last war when Japan was our ally; and let us not forget that there may be another war, and when the wheel of fate stops at the next war, the Japanese may again be our allies-who knows? If so, these little brown devils of to-day will be the little brown heroes of twenty-five years hence. I have here an excerpt from a news report which appeared in the Vancouver Province of February 24, 1920, dateline Victoria, B.C. It tells of a delegation which waited upon the provincial cabinet urging that the franchise be given in British Columbia to naturalized Canadians who fought in the great war. It says:
Leading the delegation was A. M. Whiteside, as counsel, while official support of the Vancouver branch of the great war veterans association for the Japanese was voiced by Captain Ian Mackenzie in his capacity as president.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext: That is quite right. It is well known.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext:
The quotation goes on:
It was pointed out to the government that 195 sons of Nippon-
They were called sons of Nippon in those
days.
-had gone overseas from British Columbia in the ranks of the Canadian Expeditionary Force as naturalized British subjects. Out of tips number 54 had given their lives in the allied cause and all but 12 of the remainder had been wounded more or less seriously. It was a matter therefore, it was stated, for the government at the moment to make provision in the Provincial Elections Act for 142 members of the Canadian Japanese Association. ^ British subjects wearing the returned soldier's button, to share the full privilege of British citizenship as expressed by the right to vote.
Captain (Ian) Mackenzie, in answer to a question from the Hon. William Sloan asking what effect he expected the granting of such-a request would have on the position of Hindus in British Columbia who had served with the imperial forces, replied that for the time being the great war veterans' association was not so much concerned with the details as with the general principles upon which the plea of the Canadian Japanese association was based.
I wish hon. members would think more of principles to-day than of details. Then listen to this. He goes on to say:
In his opinion these British subjects have vindicated the fundamental essentials of citizenship and an acceptance of that principle lay in the extension of the franchise.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext: A good speech.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext:
I fully agree with Captain Mackenzie, as he was then, because then he accepted and spoke on behalf of t'he principles of democracy. Let me say that the Japanese are no less to-day than they were in 1920. They are the sa.me people, and they have demonstrated that wherever they have been allowed to fight on our side during this war that they can fight bravely. There was a battalion, if that is the proper term, of Japanese Americans who fought with the American army in Italy, and it was the most decorated unit of the American army.
I do not wish at the moment to say much more on this question. I think I have definitely demonstrated that this committee cannot in logic, in justice, or in common sense maintain the position that my hon. friends from British Columbia are trying to maintain.
There was one other peculiar statement made in this debate. It was made by the hon. member for Nanaimo, a Canadian who still
Canadian Citizenship

speaks with an English accent; consequently we would expect him to retain some of those principles of democracy that Englishmen usually carry with them, though perhaps not as conspicuously as they should in their dealings with Asiatics. The hon. member for Nanaimo suggested that the proper thing, the Christian thing, I think he said, was to send these people to Japan as missionaries to teach the Japanese our Canadian way of life. Bash a man in the face, kick him in the pants, and then tell him to go back to where he or his ancestors came from and tell his countrymen what a fine fellow you are. Yes, to preach the gospel, as someone behind me suggests, of brotherly love. I suggest to the hon. member, that if he has not done so already, he should read Bruce Hutchison's column on this subject, which appeared I think in the Free Press. Bruce Hutchison is no friend of mine, but I could not have put it better myself.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext: Can the hon. member tell me the page of Hansard that he is referring to? I do not think I have been quite correctly quoted.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend the page number, but if he will look it up before I sit down, or after I sit down, and if what I have said is not correct, I will apologize humbly. But why delude ourselves with the idea that if we are foolish enough to send Japanese Canadians out of this country, they will be missionaries for our way of life? They will in fact be missionaries for a way of life which is not ours. There may be only a few of them, but the international implications of what we are doing at this time may be of supreme importance-of far more profound importance than the implications of arresting and keeping in detention without trial a few people here; although I am not condoning that act. Asia is a large continent, with an enormous population who have become pretty well tired of the white man's "superiority". Now, with the instruments of war which we have invented and which they can use just as well as we can, it may not be a good thing for the world if we goad them too far. So I suggest that in anything further we have to say in regard to this citizenship bill we try to think of Canadian citizens not according to the colour of their skin, the slant of their eyes, or the country from which they came, but as human beings.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS

I have finished, Mr. Chairman; thank you. But I wish to call the attention of the hon. member for Nanaimo to the fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg North has found the page for me, and if you will pardon me I will read the paragraph to which I referred; it is on page 704:
I think from the high Christian point of view now is the opportunity to repatriate the Japanese back to their homeland where perhaps they would be able to introduce to Japan, which has suffered so much, some of the western and Christian ideas that they have learned and in this way raise the standard of the other Japanese. They can do a great missionary work there. If they have not assimilated the ideals of western civilization while they have been here, they never will, and we should send them back.
There is no indication, Mr. Chairman, that the Japanese Canadians have not assimilated the ideals of civilization, but there are disturbing indications that people who talk in that way have not assimilated the ideals of Christian civilization.

The
Japanese of course are the largest group of dual nationality citizens we have in Canada. In reply to the hon. member I may say that this resolution was passed and submitted to the provincial command by the Vancouver East unit No. 68. The government has a particularly difficult job on its hands trying to satisfy everyone from British Columbia, but actually, it seems to me, the solution is simple. If they can satisfy one province in confederation with regard to its very simple demand, that the Japanese be excluded for a specified number of years, something that was actually promised, I should think they would leap to that opportunity. The other night when we reached section 46 I offered an amendment which, had it been accepted by the government, would have given us power

to keep the Japanese out of the Pacific coast area for the next twenty years. Why the government showed such undue enthusiasm, such unnecessary enthusiasm in getting out Beauchesne's fire extinguisher to put that out, I do not know. As a matter of fact in the election campaign the government was definitely committed on the point that the Japanese would be kept from that coast for a period of years. The undertaking at the time was that they would be kept away in perpetuity, but we are willing to concede a small point in that regard, and this is an opportunity for the government to implement that promise. I am quite sure the Minister of Veterans Affairs would be particularly happy if the promise were carried out.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have suffered from such a ruling three or four times and so have others. I respectfully submit, sir, that if you sit quietly and allow members to spend twenty-five or thirty or forty minutes on a question, presenting one side, and then refuse anyone else in the committee permission to present the other side, you are certainly giving a decision which it is difficult for anyone to understand, and certainly it does not conduce to anything ' like frank, free and fair discussion in the house. If this sort of thing goes on, how can any hon. member answer any point that is made against him? Undoubtedly, from the point of viewT of British Columbia, there is no more urgent question to be discussed at the present time than this one. I am not questioning the ruling, but I certainly think it is time to draw attention to this situation. With all respect I suggest to the chairman that if he wishes to cleave to the rules he should prevent anyone from making any attack and not stop the man who is beginning to defend himself.

May I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the member for Vancouver East has listened to attack after attack, not only upon himself as a member from British Columbia who takes a view opposed to the views held by other members from that province, but upon the party with which he is associated. He waited patiently until the time came when he could reply to those attacks, and I believe you were quite justified in permitting the reply. Now, however, it is a question whether further discussion is to be 
had, and if attacks are made replies will have to be permitted. The chair was quite justified, in my opinion, in allowing the member for Vancouver East to reply when attacks were made upon him. I think the committee will agree that this a fair statement of the case.

speechtext: I would point out that it was thoroughly understood that the member for Vancouver East would have an opportunity to speak on that particular section, and I happened to be in the chair at the time. He did rise to speak on another section, and an amendment was moved and carried and he was not allowed to speak. In all fairness I think he should have been allowed to take advantage of this opportunity to present his case. May I make this further remark. I suggest that the remark made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni with reference to the ruling on the amendment was entirely uncalled for. There are rules in this house, and it does not matter who happens to be in the chair, the chair will always, I believe, try to be fair and to stick to the rules. The amendment which the hon. member proposed at that time was completely out of order. I was in the chair at the time and I so ruled, and if I were in the chair again under the same circumstances I would have to give the same ruling. I do not think it is right to speak of "Beauchesne's fire extinguisher"; it is not fair.

I would not think of shutting off discussion if I have allowed some hon. member to take advantage of the rules. The hon. gentleman's point is well taken. I must say, however, that it shows the difficulty which arises when an hon. member departs from the rules. It prolongs debate unnecessarily. For that reason I would ask all hon. members to try to abide by the rules. I hesitate to interrupt an hon. member unless it is absolutely necessary, and hon. gentlemen can assist greatly by resolving to abide by the rules, more particularly the rule that all speeches in committee must be relevant to the clause under consideration. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggested that the hon. member for Vancouver East had been attacked time and again in the house. If that was so, the hon. member should have risen at the time and not have waited for some other clause to come up before rising to discuss what had taken place days before. I hope that from now on all hon. members will discuss the sections under consideration. The section under consideration at the present time is section 17, which has to do with dual nationality.

I thank you for your ruling, and also for the opportunity which you are giving me, and I shall try to abide by your ruling. With regard to the hon. gentleman who was acting as chairman the other night, may I say that if he took exception to the remarks I just made he must have misunderstood what I said. My reference was to what I thought was the great activity that the members of the cabinet displayed that evening. Three of them were in the house, and they displayed considerable interest in what. was going on. So far as his decision is concerned I am certain it was well and fairly given.
With reference to this question of dual nationality, I would point out that the difficulty has arisen from the fact that we cannot get any definite answer from the government. If they would give us an answer "yes" or "no", we would know where we stand. The people of Comox-Alberni believe that the Japanese are going to drift back to British Columbia. Until we have had some word from the government one way or the other I am afraid we shall have to ask them certain questions on every opportunity that presents itself.
There is an excellent precedent of this house for an evasion on the Japanese issue. I had occasion to browse through Hansard of 1908, and I found that there was a long discussion on the Japanese question. At that time we were having trouble with the Japanese in British Columbia. In 1908 the present Prime Minister was deputy minister of labour, and he came out to British Columbia to try to solve the problem. I find from Hansard of January 1908 that the Conservative party of the day was trying to get an answer from the government. The discussion ranged over a few hundred pages of Hansard, but the government was pretty light on its feet at that time too. It is curious to find that a certain Mr. Owen, a member of parliament of that day finally got the minister driven into a comer. He asked this question :
Will the hon. minister tell the house to what extent the Japanese government promised to restrict immigration?
The Hon. Mr. Lemieux, who was postmaster general at that time, said:
My hon. friend is too inquisitive. I will not answer, not from disrespect for him but because if I did answer, I would commit an act unworthy of a Canadian representative, and unworldly of myself.	-
I hope that the government is not going to take the same position at this time. They should have learned somethiug in forty years.

We shall get along. All that the British Columbia people are asking for is a definite statement. The government, which is just as much responsible to the people of British Columbia as it is to the Japanese citizens, should give that answer. I can tell the committee quite definitely that if Japanese people are allowed to come back to British Columbia there is going to be trouble. This government owes it to our Japanese residents in Canada to protect them to that extent. In my own constituency we had the Pacific coast militia rangers during the war. They did an excellent job of seeing to it that the Japanese did not invade us from the west, and they are equally determined at the present time that we are not going to be invaded from the east. The government should bear that fact in mind, because they owe the Japanese that protection.
I am not going to ask the indulgence of the committee to say any more at this time, but I did intend to say something further on the Japanese question.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS

The purpose of the resolution, and of the bill that will be based upon it, is to provide legislation to govern the conduct of crown companies. There are a-number of crown companies which were established during the war years, which have now been liquidated, or are in process of liquidation, but there are three which will, I think, continue for a considerable period, and two others which will require to continue for a time at least.
During the war, some thirty-one crown companies were incorporated under part I of the Companies Act, 1934, to carry out special projects. Some of these companies, such as Polymer Corporation Limited and Canadian Arsenals Limited, will continue their operations for a considerable period. It may also be desirable, where statutory authority exists, to incorporate similar companies to carry out other special projects.
The present bill is intended to provide for the financing of such companies and in particular to enable them to use operating revenue to pay operating costs, and to enable emergency requirements for funds to be mef; to define their status as agents of His Majesty; to make the usual provisions as to superannuation and other rights of civil servants who become employees of the company; to authorize the companies to set up pension and other welfare plans for employees who are not under the Civil Service Superannuation Act; to provide expressly for the application of the Government Employees Compensation Act to employees of the companies; and to provide for the making of annual and other reports by the companies.
Crown companies were an invention of the Department of Munitions and Supply in the early days of the war to provide a method for carrying out duties which could only be carried out with difficulty by the staff of the department. Hon. members will appreciate that, at the commencement of the war, the Department of Munitions and Supply had no staff. It was a newly created department, and it acquired its staff by going out into the highways and byways and inducing men with high patriotic purpose, men of skill and
experience, to leave their civilian occupations and join the service of the government for the period of the war.
One of the first problems encountered was the establishment of a chemicals and explosives industry in this country adequate for war. Obviously the first and paramount requirement of war is an adequate supply of ammunition and explosives. We had a chemical industry in this country and that chemical industry was used to the full, but, in addition to that, it was necessary to establish new sources of supplies for chemicals, and to establish large-scale plants for the manufacture of explosives. A very large construction problem was involved,-ultimately requiring an expenditure of more than $100 million for new construction of chemical and explosive plants.
It seemed obvious to the department that it must enlist men of great ability to carry out that programme,-men who were able to command the special skills which would be required to make the programme a success. In looking about for ways and means of organizing that programme, the department hit upon the plan of organizing a crown corporation. Thus Allied War Supplies Limited became the first of the administrative type of crown companies.
Allied War Supplies Limited is now in process of liquidation, having carried out its obligations; and we can look back on the operation of that company with a good deal of pride. It built some magnificent plants; it produced chemicals and explosives in excess of the programme set for it; the work was ' carried out at reasonable cost; every obligation was met; and after war requirements ceased considerable earnings were obtained by sale of products produced by the plants, which helped in liquidating the cost of the projects; in fact several very expensive projects have been liquidated by the sale of the product into peace-time world markets. I shall be glad to go into that operation in more detail when the bill is before the house. I mention the work of Allied War Supplies Limited at this time as an example of the purpose of the crown companies and the manner in which that work was carried out.
Crown companies divide themselves into three classes. The first class includes the administrative and supervisory companies. Allied was in that class. It did not directly operate plants, but it supervised their building, arranged for the operation of the plants, and handled the sale of the product, A number of crown companies were in that class. In

[DOT] second class were the manufacturing companies. We found as the war proceeded that it was necessary to increase the manufacture of certain products beyond the capacity of private industry to provide the service, and certain plants were built and operated directly by the government, through crown companies, to manufacture certain products. Research Enterprises Limited is an example of that class of plant. Another is Small Arms Limited, which produced vast quantities of small arms such as rifles and Sten guns. There are several other examples of crown companies established for the purpose of actually manufacturing.
Then there was the third class of companies, companies engaged in merchandising certain raw materials and in providing stockpiles sufficient to assure adequate supplies for war and civilian purposes. An example is Melbourne Merchandising company, which purchased the wool requirements of the country, stock-piled the wool and made it available to manufacturers during the war period. That company is now being liquidated. Another is Fairmont company, which performed the same duty in relation to rubber and allied products. A third is Wartime Me'tals, which was charged with the duty of keeping on hand an ample supply of metals not obtainable in Canada, such as tin and manganese. This company also undertook the expansion from Canadian sources of rare metals such as chrome, molybdenite, tungsten," mercury, and provided from Canadian sources sufficient supplies to meet all requirements during the war period. This company, Wartime Metals, is now fully liquidated.
One of the inducements for adopting the crown company plan was that it permitted men with business responsibilities of their own to give a good deal of their time to the government, in executive positions associated with a form of administration with which they were wholly familiar. The corporation is an accepted unit of Canadian business. Corporate practice is well understood'by those engaged in private business. The corporate system of accounting is also well understood and has been highly perfected through experience over the years. Therefore, to bring into being a form of organization which was readily understood, to make it sufficiently flexible so that the head office could be established in a location mo9t convenient to those men whom we wished to attract to the business, and to secure other advantages which appealed to us at the time, were the
rMr. Howe.]
determining factors which led us to carry out a number of war operations through the agency of crown companies.
The crown companies during the war years were carried on in part under the War Measures Act and were financed from the war appropriation. The finances of each company were carefully segregated. I shall be glad to give the house, when the bill is before us, a financial statement on any one of the thirty-one operations which were carried out through crown companies. Each company was expected so to conduct its business that it would not be operating in red ink. In other words, each crown company was carrying out a business operation and it was expected so to conduct its business that receipts would at least cover expenditures.
Some of these companies have been amazingly successful. As far as war work was concerned, they sold to the Canadian government and to our allies at cost, but there were certain transactions outside the purely war field which were carried on at a profit. Many of the crown companies were wound up having considerable balances on the profit side, all of which were turned over to the crown in the form of a final dividend, or alternatively were used to reduce the cost of the product to the crown. The administrative companies had no direct means of obtaining revenues even though their business was carried out in such a manner that the plants whose administration they directed were themselves profitable. The administrative companies would show chargeable to them the cost of administration without offset of earnings. In order to determine the results of companies of that type, it would be necessary to look beyond the balance sheet of the company management itself, and examine the balance sheet of the plants which it built and administered. The breakdown there is in some cases difficult to arrive at, but I think I shall be able to satisfy the house as to the results that were obtained by companies of an administrative type.
Of the thirty-one companies, seventeen have ceased operation and are either wound up or very nearly so; nine are in process of winding up, and only five are still active. The five companies that are still active are Canadian Arsenals Limited, Polymer Corporation Limited, Park Steamships Limited, Wartime Housing Limited, and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. Of these five I anticipate that Canadian Arsenals, the Polymer Corporation and Eldorado Mining and Refining will continue as crown companies for many years to come. I also anticipate that the Park

Government Companies
steamships company and Wartime Housing will be w'ound up within the next three or four years at the maximum.
We are now asking that the crown company organization be formalized. In doing so we are making provision for a form of organization that has its own uses in the work of government, particularly as the work of government becomes more complex. I quite agree that the work of crown companies should be examined by a parliamentary committee from year to year. The war expenditures committee was charged with that function during the war years, and it may be that a committee similar to the committee on railways and shipping, government-owned, or perhaps the same committee, should examine the accounts of the crown companies from year to year. However, the books of all crown companies are kept by treasury officers of the government, and all accounts and transactions are audited by the auditor general of Canada, so that members of the house can feel every assurance that the creation of a crown company does not in any way weaken the ordinary safeguards that apply to government business.
One difficulty in analysing government-owned business in general is the government's method of bookkeeping. It is a simple method of bookkeeping. Everything that is paid out by the treasury is charged up as expenditures from a government appropriation and everything that is received is entered on the books as revenue. In a business, it is difficult to provide incentives with that kind of bookkeeping. Unless the corporation can be charged with its expenditures, and has to account for those expenditures, and at the same time receives credit for its income, and be expected to have the income side in excess over the expenditure side and be required to answer questions to a parliamentary committee if the reverse is the case, I think we lose a good deal in incentive to the personnel that is carrying on that particular government business.
The bill that will be based on this resolution provides for the normal corporation accounting for crown companies. I think that is an important feature of the measure. It also makes provision for the welfare of the employees of crown companies. These men are not civil servants, unless they have been transferred to the company from the permanent civil service. In cases where they have been transferred, the bill makes provision for their civil service protection to be continued. In the case of employees recruited outside the civil service, the bill provides for the benefits that are usual in similar private undertakings.
The bill has been carefully drawn. It is simple in form, and contains only those provisions that are required for the normal business of the corporation. At the same time, I believe the bill contains all the safeguards that parliament will require. However, hon. members can judge that for themselves when the bill is brought down, and I shall be glad to reserve for that occasion anything more I have to say.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: I have just two questions to ask the minister. His resolution states that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the operation and financing of government companies, which the minister has referred to as crown companies. I presume this measure is made necessary because the companies were set up under the War Measures Act?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: Under the Companies Act.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: And now they are continued under the emergency powers legislation?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: They were set up under the dominion Companies Act, part I. They were operated to some extent under the War Measures Act, and were financed from the war appropriations voted by parliament. Therefore, since there are no more war appropriations, it is desirable that separate provision be made for finances and for operating method.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext:
That brings me to the point of my first question. If some legislation of this kind was not needed before, what is the special need for it now? Perhaps the minister will make that clear after I am through.
The other question is this. One of the purposes of the measure is said to be to define the status of these crown companies as agents to His Majesty and to provide further for the superannuation, pension or other rights of the employees of such companies. I had gathered from the resolution that these companies were not to be permanent institutions. Apparently they are either temporary or semi-temporary institutions. Would the minister explain why it is necessary to provide for superannuation, pension and so on in crown companies that, so far as we know, are intended only to be short-lived? There must be some thought that they will be long-lived institutions. These are the two points I had in mind to ask about.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext:
In reply to the first point, the particular need is to provide a method of financing for the companies. During the war the funds required by the companies were withdrawn from the war appropriation that
Government Companies

had been voted by parliament, and the receipts of the company were paid into the consolidated revenue fund. The companies had no right to retain in their possession funds beyond those required for operating. In other words, the companies worked on appropriations and paid their surplus funds into the consolidated revenue fund. This bill will enable each company to accumulate from its earnings the funds which can be used for the expenses of the company and would be held for that purpose to the extent of operational requirements.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: The effect is to remove them still farther from parliament.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext:
No; to bring them closer, if you like. The method of bookkeeping proposed is much easier for parliament to check than the method in the usual government accounting. I think that fact will appear when we examine the bill.
As regards the permanency of the companies, we have continuing operations that in my judgment will be better continued under an organization of this type. One is the Polymer Corporation, a vast chemical plant built for the manufacture of synthetic rubber to meet emergent war needs. It was built at a cost of about $50 million. In addition to the manufacture of rubber, certain byproducts of the process are being sold as a basis for a great separate organic chemical industry. Already two or three important privately owned chemical plants are either in operation or are being constructed to purchase by-products of the Polymer plant. The Polymer operation is a tremendous undertaking, and I think it would be folly to attempt the operation without using a corporate form for the enterprise.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: That is a new crown company which is in contemplation?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: No; the Polymer Corporation was created to build and operate the synthetic rubber plant at Sarnia.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: The minister spoke about a new chemical company.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: The Polymer Corporation built its plant and has operated it for the past three years.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: The new chemical developments mentioned are to be carried on by Polymer?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext:
No; these are private developments. They will purchase as their new material certain by-products resulting from the preparation of the material for the Polymer process which were surplus to the require-

ments of the Polymer. These are becoming the basis of a substantial organic chemical industry in the same area. Private expansion in the organic chemical field will continue, I believe, and should the requirements of synthetic rubber be curtailed at any time it would prove to be a way of saving the government's investment by providing a market for the products that are at present the base materials for synthetic rubber.
Another crown company that will continue is the Dominion Arsenals Limited. Before the war, it was the practice to operate the arsenals as a branch of government. All the employees were civil servants, and the operations were carried on by civil service practice. An appropriation was made by parliament to cover the expenditures and any receipts were paid into the consolidated revenue fund. At present the arsenals are being operated as a crown company. There is a reasonable chance that the earnings of the arsenals will pay their operating expenses, and that an appropriation from parliament from year to year will not be needed, which will certainly be a welcome change in the pre-war arsenal situation. I shall be glad to explain the composition of Dominion Arsenals when we consider the bill. I believe that present arrangements are a great improvement in the method of operating continuing dominion government arsenals between wrars.
A third company that should continue in corporate form is Eldorado Mining and Refining. This is a mining operation in a remote area in the northwest territories. It is one of the world's great suppliers of uranium and radium.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: What about their outside properties?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext:
All the Eldorado properties are owned by the Eldorado Corporation. This is the third corporation under the Companies Act which I think will be a continuing operation, at least as long as it is desirable the production of uranium be under strict government control.
I might explain the difference between a crown company referred to in this bill and other government companies. For example. War Assets Corporation is not a corporation under the Qompanies Act; it is a corporation created by act of parliament. That is the only company associated with the Department of Munitions and Supply, that is not a company under the Companies Act. This bill does not refer to the operation of War Assets Corporation.

Government Companies

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext:

The government has control over the appointment of personnel, salaries of personnel and matters such as superannuation and pension plans in the present regulations governing the company.
The need for a reasonable superannuation and pension plan will be apparent in the case of Polymer. Polymer is located alongside the Imperial Oil refinery at Sarnia. The type of employee is much the same as the type of employee of the Imperial Oil refinery. Hon. members are no doubt aware that Imperial Oil has an advanced policy in the matter of superannuation and benefits to its employees. It would hardly be practical for the government to carry on a similar operation alongside without having some plan of a corresponding nature. The same is true of the arsenals. In my opinion the number of civil servants in the arsenals should be reduced rather than expanded, and protection afforded by means of an adequate retirement and benefit plan. The same is true also of Eldorado.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: Does the minister anticipate that more than the three companies he has mentioned will be of a permanent nature?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: The department over which I preside has plans for only the three companies mentioned, although two other companies will require at least two or three years to liquidate their obligations.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: Which ones are they?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: Park Steamships is one and Wartime Housing is another.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: Will these social security plans be the same for all three companies?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: Not necessarily. The needs of different industries vary and each industry has its own pattern for social security. In some industries it may be desirable to have an earlier retiring age than in others, and other industries may require a different type of benefit. It has been the practice to permit the management to work out its benefit plan with its employees, and the companies have not been held to a standard pattern.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: Has the minister any figures as to the number of employees in each of these corporations? I am concerned at the moment only with the Polymer Corporation, Dominion Arsenals and Eldorado.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me to give that information on the next occasion this matter is considered?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext:
I have a couple of questions to ask, but before doing so I wish to bring something to the attention of the committee. I would not like to see what took place in connection with this debate become a precedent. Before Mr. Speaker left the chair the hon. member for Eglinton was on his feet and he certainly had the right to speak. He tried to speak but Mr. Speaker simply left the chair. The rights of hon. members should be respected and any hon. member who wants to rise to his feet to speak should be permitted to do so. Before we vote money on anything like this we should have an opportunity to have Mr. Speaker in the chair. I just bring that up in passing.
In connection with the Polymer Corporation, I should like to know the price per pound at which synthetic rubber is selling. I should also like to know if the plants of Dominion Arsenals are to be operated as pilot plants for experimental work. If so, how does the minister expect to make a profit? Perhaps he can give this information later on when the bill is before the house.

speechtext: My recollection is that synthetic rubber sells at 20J cents a pound.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext:
How does that compare with the price of natural rubber?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: Natural rubber has been selling for 45 cents a pound but I think the price of new importations is 24 cents a pound f.o.b. Malaya. I presume that would permit it to be laid down in Canada for about 30 cents a pound, or perhaps a little less. I am sure of the price at which synthetic rubber is selling but I am giving the other figures from memory.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: Will our Canadian plant be able to compete in the future with the "supplies of natural rubber?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext:
The fact that the government owns a synthetic rubber plant will not be used to deprive anyone from the privilege of purchasing natural rubber. Natural rubber is brought in without duty, and there is no obstacle to trade.
In my opinion nothing should interfere with the right of Canadian industry to purchase either synthetic or natural rubber. At the moment, even though the synthetic rubber plant is producing considerably in excess of its rated capacity, it is unable to supply the demands of Canadian industry. When the plant was built, it was tailored to meet war requirements, which we believed would be about double peace-time requirements, but the fact is that the full capacity of the plant is being used to meet peace-time requirements, just as it was used during the war years to meet war-time requirements. There is no indication on the horizon that there will be any change in the situation, at least for two years. Reports indicate that the natives in the jungle seem to have wakened up to the fact that they can'sell their labour for money, and it seems doubtful whether they will be prepared to produce rubber for the low wages that prevailed in pre-war days.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext: Just what is proposed in connection with the Canadian arsenals? Are these plants to be operated as pilot plants for experimental work?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext:
The plants of Dominion
Arsenals were never primarily experimental plants. They produce the requirements of the army in times of peace. Their work consisted partly of the overhaul of equipment, partly of the development of new equipment and partly of the replacement of wastage caused by the wear and tear of army manoeuvres in time of peace. As I have said, in former days an appropriation was voted for Dominion Arsenals and any work was charged against that appropriation until it was exhausted.
It is now proposed that Dominion Arsenals will charge the army, the navy and the air force for the work allocated to each arsenal.
[Mt. D. G. Ross.]
The work will carry with it a price, just as it did in war-time, and it is expected that the tvork performed in the arsenals will provide sufficient revenue to pay the expenses of operating. For instance, one arsenal plant is now producing ammonia nitrate fertilizer and selling it in the world market. It is also producing other chemicals which are being sold at a profit, and the total profits on this one operation are at present well over $1,000,000 a year, which is quite a contribution toward the cost of carrying the entire arsenals programme.
Another arsenal plant is engaged in overhauling 25-poundet guns for the army. That is an army contract which carries with it the same price it would have carried in wartime. The revenue the arsenal is drawing from that price will also help to carry the cost of the arsenal programme. Similarly, orders for ammunition are placed from time to time; perhaps not just at the present time, but they have been for years and doubtless will be again. That ammunition will be sold at a reasonable commercial price, and there again the proceeds will go into the arsenal fund.
It is my hope-perhaps it is rather a bold hope at this time, or until such time as we have more experience-that the work performed by the arsenals, paid for at reasonable commercial rates, will provide sufficient revenue to cover all costs of the arsenals, and perhaps provide a surplus which can be paid into the consolidated revenue fund.

speechtext: While this resolution would appear to be a most innocuous one, I submit it represents an unusual advance in the direction of the government's going into business.

speechtext: I note that there is applause from the C.C.F corner of the house, indicating that the minister will get support from that direction-

speechtext:
-in the stand
which he has taken. I suggest that at some time during the discussion on the resolution the minister should let the country know to what extent the government intends to carry into effect a policy of that kind, or of going into or continuing in business in competition with private industry.
If the government is going into business, has consideration been given to the fact that it should accept the responsibilities ordinarily accepted by private industry? Has con-

Government Companies
sideration been given to the removal of the principle which has been in effect for many hundreds of years, namely that the crown cannot be sued. If the government is going into business, through the setting up of crown companies, in any bill introduced provision should be made so that suit can be brought against such companies, in the same way as against private industry.
Then, if the government is going into business should the ancient principle, that which states that because a company is a crown company it should not be subject to municipal or other taxation, be continued? If the government is going into competition with private business, or if it is going to operate industry by itself, should it depart from what is ordinarily accepted to be the ambit of government operations?
Is it not time to place in this measure a provision permitting that crown companies be sued, and that they be placed on an equality with corporations operated privately by their being required to make payments of taxation.
I suggest that the minister should reply to these points, because they are of peculiar importance at this time, owing to the fact that apparently the government has decided, in days of peace, to carry into effect a system of crown companies which operated in time of war. The minister has pointed out that they operated successfully in war time and that, generally speaking, they returned a profit. One can understand that. But we are now in days of peace, and we know that all crown corporations have not in the past returned profits. The fact that they are crown corporations does not necessarily establish any assumption that they will be successfully operated for the benefit of the public. I mention only one company-and I shall not discuss its affairs in detail-but if there is any corporation in the country criticized to-day, then certainly that corporation is War Assets Corporation. The people as a whole find it difficult to get any replies from it, and on many occasions to get service from it. Indeed, as someone suggests to me, even members of parliament experience the same difficulty; and that is a condition which I believe is general on all sides of the house.
I should appreciate the minister's outlining generally the adoption of any new type of policy by the government, so that the committee and the country will know just to what extent the government has decided to adopt socialistic principles at this time.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING
speechtext:
I was called a socialist in the early days of the war, and now I am called a capitalist because I am liquidating socialized organizations. We built some government-operated plants, to a value of nearly S900 million. During the last few years we have liquidated the larger portion, as far as government ownership and operation are concerned.
We would be glad to sell the Polymer Corporation to private industry, if private industry would buy it. We built it to serve a great national need, particularly to serve a war need. It has been a successful undertaking, and is now operating at a substantial profit. It has already paid back in profits some $10 million of the $50 million. We are selling rubber at the ceiling price. We are prepared to meet competition for some time to come. However, I believe the manufacture of synthetic rubber by the government of Canada is for the general advantage of Canadian business. I have yet to hear any business man suggest it was not a good thing for Canadian business to have Canada's only source of rubber in the hands of the government, rather than in the hands of a private corporation.
The government has no intention of going into business unnecessarily. Occasions have arisen in the past where it was important and, I suggest, imperative, that the government go into business on a very large scale. Such occasions may occur again, and if they do I hope the government of that day will be bold enough to meet the situation. This fetish, in the minds of some people, that everything is wrong that is private industry, and in the minds of others that everything is wrong that is public industry, is a most ridiculous situation. Fortunately I am a Liberal, and hold no such theories. I regret to observe that my hon. friends across the way seem to be divided into groups that are unanimous, either on one side or on the other.
Might I remind hon. members that in a speech on March 31, 1943, Mr. Churchill offered the following observation:
If we act with comradeship and loyalty to our country and to one another, and if we can make state enterprise and free enterprise both serve the national interest, and pull the wagon side by side, there is no need to fear.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF WORKS CONSTRUCTED AS OF JUNE 1, 1938

speechtext: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works) moved the second reading of bill No. 9, to amend the Navigable Waters' Protection Act.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF WORKS CONSTRUCTED AS OF JUNE 1, 1938
speechtext: Before this bill is read a second time I should like to ask the minister a question. The purpose, as I understand it, of part I of the Navigable Waters' Protection Act is to prevent our navigable rivers from being obstructed or impeded or rendered dangerous or difficult for ships by the construction of bridges or wharves or dams or other structures which have not been approved by the governor in council. This is necessary and important legislation. The amendment that is proposed is an amendment of subsection 2 of section 5 of the act, which I have just had an opportunity to look at for a minute, and provides that before any obstruction can be put in navigable waters permission has to be obtained of the governor in council. If permission is not obtained from the governor in council, if my recollection serves me correctly-I have not had the time to look carefully into this just now-there is provision that permission can subsequently be obtained; and if I understand it, the amendment which is proposed has to do with that permission. Am I right in that supposition? Is the amendment to provide for permission in the cases of works which have been put up without the consent of the governor in council?

subtopic: APPROVAL OF WORKS CONSTRUCTED AS OF JUNE 1, 1938
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF WORKS CONSTRUCTED AS OF JUNE 1, 1938
speechtext: May I ask, then, why the date has been changed; why this amendment is being made? Have certain works been constructed without the approval of the governor in council which this amendment is intended to cover and, if that is so, for what particular works is this amendment to provide?

subtopic: APPROVAL OF WORKS CONSTRUCTED AS OF JUNE 1, 1938
speechtext:
As the hon. member has mentioned, the amendment proposed in this bill is a change of the date mentioned in subsection 2 of section 5. The act itself came into effect in 1886, and it was

Navigable Waters
151*
passed for reasons of security and defence purposes, to ensure that there were no obstacles or impediments in navigable waters so that in case of emergency or in case of war navigation would be free in those waters.. The act has not been amended very often since 1886, but on a few occasions parliament has approved the change of the date in subsection 2 of section 5. It actually reads:
The governor in council may approve of works constructed, or in process of construction, on the first day of June, one thousand nine hundred and eighteen, subject to the provisions of section seven hereof, and such approval shall have the same effect as approval of works to be constructed.
That refers to section 7 of part I of the Navigable Waters' Protection Act. I may state here that the first part of the act comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works; the two other sections of the act come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges). The first part relates to works that are "built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site thereof has been approved by the governor in council," or "unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council." On account of war conditions, this section has not been amended for a good many years. I cannot recall whether it was 1926 or 1928 when the last amendment was made. But I am informed that certain works since 1918 have been put up without approval of the sites or of the works being asked from the Department of Public Works, and it is thought that we should now change this date to June 1, 1938.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TWO RACE MEETS AT ONE TRACK

speechtext:
Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second [DOT] reading of bill No. 15, to amend the criminal code (race meetings).
He said: Perhaps I should make an explanation of this bill before we go into committee. It was introduced in the senate, partly for the purpose of expediting the work of the session, and received its introduction as a result of representations made from the Department of Agriculture.
When the bill was introduced it was the intention to make two amendments, the most important of which is contained in section 2 of the bill. This amendment provides for having two race meets held, or the race meets of two different associations held on one track. Prior to the war an association held a race meet of seven days on its track. During the war we found it necessary to use some of these race track accommodations, and it was found advisable to have two meets held on one track. It has been found that there is no objection to that. As a matter of fact, many things can be said in favour of it, both by those who favour racing and by those who do not. It is proposed that what has been in the order in council throughout the war should now be placed in the legislation itself.
While that legislation was being prepared, it was proposed to eliminate, or to make it impossible for those who had had a charter under the old situation which existed prior to 1912, to operate. Charters were given under different conditions. A law was passed about that time compelling all those who wanted to have a charter for racing to have legislation
Criminal Code

either federal or provincial. It was thought that we might eliminate from pari-mutuels all those who had been organized for the purpose of having trotting and pacing races. But it has been represented to me by hon. members from both sides of the house that only one organization is affected by it, that some hardship would be created so far as it is concerned, and that no particular good would be done by bringing about a change at this time.
Therefore, when we are in committee I intend to move an amendment to remove the words "other than an association empowered by its charter to conduct only trotting and pacing races or to maintain and operate a driving park." Those words having been asked to be eliminated, the section will be in exactly the same position as it was before, with the exception of three words in line 6 near the top of page 2, which are only to clarify the meaning. No change is brought about by them.
Therefore the important change is in section 2, which makes it possible for two associations to hold a race meet at one park.
