subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT

speechtext:
Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of
bill No. 54, to amend the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, 1942.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: Is the minister going to explain the bill?

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext:
I really do not think any explanation is needed apart from the explanation I made on the first reading of the bill. In 1942 an act was passed dealing with the reinstatement of men in the armed forces. I think the house will appreciate that at that time this was more or less a virgin field. In the last war there was no legislation of that description, and the act was drafted in the light of the limited experience we had at that time. I remember that I played some part in the drafting of that measure.
In the light of practical experience a number of orders in council were passed under the War Measures Act. That is, as difficulties arose and interpretations were necessary to broaden the act, they were embodied in orders in council passed under the War Measures Act; and all that this does is to give statutory authority to those regulations under the War Measures Act, because we shall need them, we expect, at the time when bill No. 15 expires.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act was passed, as the minister has said, in 1942. It was passed after careful consideration by a special committee of the house, and I think that in practice it has worked out very well. I agree with what the minister said on the first reading of the bill to the effect that employers had shown great willingness to comply with the spirit of the act and that generally speaking, the act had been very successful. The bill under consideration this evening is to amend that act and bring it up to date. Apparently in the years which have intervened since the act was passed it has been found that corrections were needed; and, as the explanatory note points out, these corrections, which were made
(Mr. Gardiner.]
by order in council are now to be incorporated in the act. On page 2 of the bill will be found these words in one of the orders in council:
That it is therefore, by reason of the war, deemed necessary, for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada, to make regulations defining the rights of persons to reinstatement in civil employment pending reconsideration of the said act by parliament.
Those last few words are the ones I want to emphasize:	"pending reconsideration of
the said act by parliament." This is what was done:	changes were made by order in
council. They were called regulations, but in effect they were changes in the act; and now I suggest to the minister that these changes should be written right into the act-[DOT]

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: In effect that is what this does.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: -whereas this bill simply takes four orders in council and makes them schedules to the act.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: That is the same thing.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext:
It does not sort out the parts of the regulations which should be written into the act. It just takes the four orders in council holus-bolus, calls them the schedule to the act, and that is aid there is to it.
This is the first time, to my knowledge, that legislation has been brought in to put orders in council into statutory form. I assume there will be other instances, both during this present session and in the sessions immediately ahead, and I think it is important that we get started in the right way. I suggest to the ministry that the practice should be to take out of the orders in council those portions which should be in the acts, and leave as regulations those parts which are really regulations. But that is not what is done here. It is particularly important that all legislation having to do with men who have served in the forces be clearly set out, so that there can be no misunderstanding of the rights of those men who have stood between us and our enemies, who have saved this country. If this bill passes in its present form their rights will not be clearly defined, because there is apt to be a conflict between the act and the regulations.
Take the soldier who reads the act. If this bill is passed in its present form, the man who goes to the act to see what his rights are, when he reads the act, will think it defines his rights. But in fact many of the most important rights which have been given to him are set out in the sjhedule. In other

Forces-Reinstatement in Employment
words, they were in the orders in council, and now, in the way this bill is drawn, they will have to be dug up out of the schedule. I would ask the ministry to look at these orders in council and see some of the examples. For example, on page 2 we find that section 3 of the regulations in that particular order in council reads:
For the purposes of the act and these regulations	
Then it goes on to make certain definitions. Section 6 deals with what shall be done where an employer operates a business in several different establishments: it is an important provision; yet it will be in the schedule and not in the original act. In section 7 of the order in council, to be found at the foot of page 3 of the bill, we find provisions for making application for reinstatement. In the bottom line the following appears:
And, notwithstanding section 4 of the act, it is not a defence in proceedings for violation of section 3 of the act for the employer to prove facts described by paragraph (b) of section 4 of the act unless he also proves that the employee applied for reinstatement before he offered reinstatement to him.
That contradicts part of the. original act and it should be written into the act.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: Look at the last section of the order in council.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: I will read that. It is the worst feature of all.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: I think it is the best.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext:
Paragraph 8 of the order in council covers application to a reinstatement officer for assistance, and we find at the bottom of page 4 another provision which protects the veteran. It takes away one of the defences given to the employer under the original act. Section 10 should also be set out in the act. It provides:
Proof, for the purposes of paragraph (e) of section 4 of the act. that an applicant was employed to take the place of an employee who had been previously accepted for service in His Majesty's forces may only be made by proving that the applicant w-as employed directly or indirectly to take the place of the other employee and would not have been employed if the other employee had not left the employment.
Section 11 is an important one that should be in the act. It relates to rate of remuneration on reinstatement and also provides for permanent status and seniority of the employee. Section 12 of this order in council provides for vacations with pay, another important feature that should be in the act.
I will not cite other instances, but there are two or three more to be found in the order in council. The order in council concludes with paragraph 17:
Where there is any conflict between the provisions of the act and the provisions of these . regulations, the regulations prevail.
All other legislation that I know of provides that the provisions of the act shall prevail over the regulations, but here we have a provision that the regulations shall prevail over the act. That was quite proper when the order in council was originally passed, because in effect it was passed as a statute under the War Measures Act. I am not quarrelling with its being there in an order in council under the War Measures Act, but I suggest that most of the provisions should really be part of the act and should be put into the act, leaving anything else as a schedule or more properly as regulations. Actually, this is careless draftsmanship on the part of somebody.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: Let me say to my hon. friend that the regulations were drafted by a gentleman like himself, a lawyer, not a layman. In any event, I thought that on the second reading we discussed the principle of the bill and not its details.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: Surely that is a principle.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext:
The second order in council, which is made part of the schedule to the bill, obviously contains provisions that should be written right into the definition section of the act itself. It is to extend the act to cover members of the naval, military or air forces of any of the united nations who were employed in Canada prior to September 9, 1939. The other two orders in council, made a part of the schedule, should also be incorporated in the definition section of the act.
I would not want the minister or the house to think I am quarrelling with the act respecting reinstatement in civil employment, or with the provisions that have been passed during the war to improve that act; but I am suggesting, in fairness to the veterans, in fairness to the men who are protected by this act, that the bill should be withdrawn and should be brought back in the form of an amendment to the original act. Not until then shall we have it in proper shape.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT

speechtext: I did not say that.

speechtext: I beg your pardon.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext: I am a humble person.

Let us therefore take just a little time out for the purpose. I think the whole house agrees with the principle and with what is sought to be done. We have here a short act and tremendous schedules, because they are tremendous, comparable with the size of the act itself, and the act means nothing; the schedules mean everything. Let us simplify our procedure, our reading and our difficulties and avoid trouble for us who are lawyers and who have to try to interpret these things that are done by non-legal persons.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext:
I rise to support what the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) have said with respect to the manner in which this bill has been brought in. I do not believe there would be any disagreement from any section of this house on the objects of the bill. As the hon. member for Vancouver South said a few moments ago, the urgency of the bill does not mean very much because it is in effect now, having regard to the legislation 
passed under the War Measures Act. However, that drives or should drive the minister into the position where this bill ought to be overhauled. It is not a question of amendment; it is a question of a complete overhaul of this bill. In my opinion this bill will create a dangerous, a clumsy and an ineffective precedent for this government and this parliament to follow. Particularly is that true at a time when we are passing from order in council legislation to ordinary parliamentary legislation.
I am perfectly serious with respect to this, because if we create this precedent now there is no reason why in the transitional period legislation may not follow the basis and the example that this legislation now sets. I am not referring particularly to the minister in this regard because he has completely exonerated himself from all possible results that may follow from this bill. This is nothing but a lazy man's legislation. As an hon. member said, from the point of view of neatness alone it should be changed, but I shall not put it on that basis. This is nothing short of simply making parliament just an ordinary bookbindery for putting together some orders in council and running them through. That is not good enough. We have to be something more than a bookbindery putting together orders in council.
We hear talk about a veterans' charter. This is nothing more than a scrapbook so far as veterans are concerned. It is making a laughing-stock of veterans' legislation. I do not think this is the kind of legislation that we should pass as the law by which the veterans of this country are to be governed, to say nothing of the employers who are to give them employment when they come back.
The schedules of ordinary legislation usually contain the aftermath of the legislation or some of the regulations and so on that go with it. But here we have the material parts of the bill not in the bill itself but in the schedule. From a reading of the bill it is obvious that it is unsound so far as procedure is concerned, because in three or four places in the bill one finds not only the numbers of the orders in council passed under the War Measures Act but also the name of the clerk of the privy council, if you please. His name is right in the legislation. If that is not an untidy piece of business, to say nothing of the operational parts of the bill, then I think the minister will have to revise his opinion as to what is good legislation.
Before second reading is given and before the bill becomes law which will serve as a precedent-and that is bothering me considerably, particularly at this psychological time, because it might be followed by this

Forces-Reinstatement in Employment
government passing a piece of legislation after a piece of legislation where we shall be simply binding up orders in council that have been passed during the war; they will be presented to the house in undigested form and we shall be asked to fill the statute books by simply putting the rubber-stamp of parliament upon orders in council that have been passed under entirely different circumstances-I would ask the minister to consider these objections to the bill. The objects are good; the idea is an excellent one and will have no possible objection from any part of the house. But when there is such unanimity with respect to the objects and the principle of the bill, please do not let us render it ineffective or pass it in a form which is much less than what a good bill deserves. For that reason I ask that this clumsy bill be overhauled and something better put in its place, something that will give effect to what we want to give effect to, namely, the objects of the legislation.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT ACT, 1942-REGULATIONS GIVEN STATUTORY EFFECT
speechtext:
I am not a lawyer, but I have listened to some of my legal friends to-night. What we need is a bill that the ordinary layman can understand. I have spoken on the floor of this house many times since 1942 in connection with veterans legislation which is to be found in chapter 31, 1942-43, of the statutes of Canada, and is entitled:
An act to provide for the reinstatement in civil employment of discharged members of His Majesty's forces and other designated classes of persons.
There is in this act a section which is most important and interesting. I shall read it. It is section 3, and reads as follows:
It shall be the duty of any employer by whom a person accepted for service in Mis Majesty's forces was employed when accepted for such service, to reinstate him in employment at the termination of his service in such occupation and position as would be consistent with the true intent and purposes of this act and under conditions not less favourable to him

Remember that.

than those which would have been applicable to him had he remained in the employment of that employer.
It is impossible to put that into effect because you do not know the individuality of the individual; you do not know what his capabilities are; you do not know how far he would have gone. He might have been general manager of the company if he had stayed there. I want to bring this to the attention of the house. The section continues:
Provided, that the right to reinstatement shall be subject to established rules of seniority in the employer's establishment, with retention of seniority rights during the employee's period of service with His Majesty's forces, or, in an absence of such rules, to preference according to dates of first employment in the employer's service with due consideration to continuity of employment in that service:	And provided,
further, that for determining the employee's rights to pension or other benefits, service in His Majesty's forces shall be deemed to have been service with the employer.
I am of the opinion that that paragraph of this act is almost impossible of accomplishment.

It seems to me this bill is so important that it should have gone to the veterans affairs committee. It is something pertaining absolutely to veterans; and if we are to have a veterans charter administered by one department and one minister, then I believe the subject matter of this bill belongs to the veterans affairs committee at this time, in order that it may be given an overhauling. There are many things wrong with it. I am not going to take time this evening to go into them all, but I would suggest to the minister that this legislation be passed along now to the veterans affairs committee. All during the war we bowed to the emergency and accepted legislation by order in council. Under the Emergency Powers Act the government still has the right to administer by order in council where there is an emergency. No emergency exists at the present time with regard to this legislation. The war is over; the soldiers are coming back. Many of them are having difficulty in getting back the jobs they left when they entered the services. Instead of the Minister of Labour continuing to try to handle this, with the many complex problems with which he has to deal in the field of employment, I believe he should be glad to pass it over to the veterans affairs committee.
I believe the time to legislate by order in council has passed. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South that simply -'incorporating all these orders in council into .this bill and making the schedule the dominant factor in it is the wrong thing to do. I am igoing to point out just one or two difficulties in connection with the provision concerning 'vacation with pay; and mind you, these difficulties exist right across the country. For example, during the war thousands of soldiers were on industrial leave. They were taken out of the services for work in coal mines and on farms, and to meet other essential requirements. They may have spent a year or eighteen months in industry before going back to the army to be discharged. Then, when they came back to industry the time they spent in industrial life did not count in connection with vacations with pay. The employer said no, the man was in the service. The army said no, he was on leave without pay. So that there is a good deal of friction in that regard. Only a few days ago the mine, mill and smelter workers' union-

Yes. In spite of the fact that a soldier on leave might have spent approximately eighteen months in a given industry he had to go back to the army to be discharged.
[Mr. Gillis.)
Then, when he came back to the industry they told him he was not entitled to a vacation with pay because he had not worked for ninety days since his discharge, overlooking the fact that he had been there for the previous eighteen months. I know the order in council states that if the employer so desires he may waive the ninety-day period and grant a vacation with pay; but the minister will remember that this subject nearly caused an upheaval in the mines of Nova Scotia, because the employers said they would not grant that vacation with pay if a man did not have the ninety days of service, unless they got a directive from the government. I do not believe it is correct to say that this particular bill was discussed by the committee on veterans affairs last year, but I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Cape Breton South has a good deal of merit, and it seems to me the arguments presented by the Progressive Conservative members have been convincing. I do not think hon. members should be asked to pass this kind of legislation. One of the orders in council was dated January 11, 1945; the next one August 2, 1945; another, November 6, 1945, and the last, April 9, 1946. Surely the minister should not proceed with this type of legislation. If he would agree to refer it
to the veterans affairs committee for redrafting, he would be supporting the general objective of the legislation.
Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton):
I do not intend to cover any of the points which have been covered so effectively thus far, but I should like to state briefly one or two things which have occurred to me.
So far as the form of the legislation is concerned, if parliament gives second reading to the bill in its present form we shall be making ourselves look foolish, not only in the eyes of the people of this country, but in the eyes of other legislatures as well. With the idea that there should be submitted to parliament certain regulations and orders passed under war-time authority, or under the authority of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, I think we are all in agreement. In other words, I believe we agree that what has the force of legislation passed under that authority should now be submitted to parliament.
But that is a very different thing from submitting these orders in council to the house, regardless of whether they are in harmony with or in contradiction of the existing statutes, and saying, "You have to take them, holus-bolus." I suggest that in its present form this bill offends every canon of legislation.
Here are the four simple rules which any bill coming before this house should clearly observe. In the first place, a bill should be a unity. In the second place, it ought to be clear in meaning. In the third place, it should be logical in construction. In the fourth place, it should not be contradictory. This bill offends each of these four canons of legislation.
In the first place, it is not a unity. What do we find in the bill? We find that we are to take what really represents five different bills. We have the original enactment of 1942, followed by the long, general regulations, of which there are seventeen in all. Attention has already been drawn to section 17, which states, in effect, that if the regulations and statute are in conflict, so much the worse for the statute.
Following that, we have three other orders in council. I should like the house to take just a minute to observe what these various steps are, in sequence. I have referred, first, to the general order in council consisting of seventeen sections. It will be noted that section 17 in the first group of regulations is not repeated in those which follow. Therefore, in giving effect now, as proposed, to section
1532	COMMONS
Forces-Reinstatement in Employment	*
17, we are not saying that the three following orders in council, if adopted, override the statute. No, we do not say that. It is only this first one.
Then we come to the next order in council of August 2, 1945, and we find there an amendment of the original act. This is an amendment to the definition section, section 2.
Then we turn to the third order in council of November 6, and find an amendment to the regulations.
Turning to the fourth order in council, we find that it is an amendment to some of the regulations set up in the third order in council. What does it mean? We say in the bill that all of these become law, and that all shall have the effect of a statute, from this time forward. We are legislating a contradiction. We are legislating with respect to this third order in council, and we are saying, "We will give this the force of a statute." Then we come along to the fourth order in council, and say, in the same breath, and under the same enactment, that part of the third order in council has not the force of law because it has been overridden by the fourth.
Is parliament going to put itself in a position of legislating a hodge-podge like that, contradictory within its own terms, anything but clear, illogical and anything but a unity. I suggest that parliament will look foolish if it proceeds to enact legislation in that fonm. If there ever was a bill which ought to be so clear that he who runs may read, then it should be legislation dealing with the rights of veterans, because the veterans are looking to this measure for their charter rights. Those rights ought to be perfectly clear for any layman to read. This is not the kind of legislation that a citizen should need to take to a lawyer for interpretation; it should be abundantly clear. But we are just going to legislate in a hodge-podge fashion if we pass this.
We have heard a useful suggestion, one which has now been endorsed by several hon. members, namely, that- the bill should go to the committee on veterans affairs, 'and should there be rewritten. All these contradictions and any repetition should be eliminated, so that when the bill comes back, with such improvement as may be worked out in the veterans affairs committee, we shall have a piece of legislation which will be sound, complete and comprehensive, and wall be free of the accusations now properly made against it, that it is not clear, that it is illogical, that it is full of contradictions.
I do not offer that in any sense in a scolding spirit. Rather, I urge upon the minister 
in charge of the bill that in this matter affecting the rights of veterans to reinstatement in civil employment we want to have a clear and comprehensive statute, and we should not pass this legislation, in its present deplorable form.

It shall be the duty of any employer by whom a person accepted for service in His Majesty's forces was employed when accepted for such service, to reinstate him in employment at the termination of his service in such occupation and position as would he consistent with the true intent and purposes of this act and under conditions not less favourable to him than those which would have been applicable to him had he remained in the employment of that employer.

Export Act

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of bill No. 14, to amend the Export Act.
He said: The purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is to eliminate certain overlapping with the Game Export Act and to assist the administration of provincial game regulations. Sections 5 and 6 of the Export Act, which this bill seeks to repeal, prohibit:
The export in the carcass, or parts thereof, of (a) deer, except as authorized by regulation of the governor in council made under the authority of the Customs Act; and (b) wild turkeys, quail, partridge, prairie fowl and woodcock.
It is contrary to law in the United States to import game which is illegally exported from Canada, and the United States and state authorities enforce this law.
Under the Export Game Act a visiting sportsman may come into Canada and shoot woodcock, wild turkey, or prairie fowl under
Export Act

a permit issued by the province, but on returning to his home in the United States he will find that he cannot import into that country the game which he legally shot in Canada. We had a case which illustrates the point very clearly. The chief game warden of New Brunswick was endeavouring last year to make arrangements with United States authorities so that United States sportsmen who lawfully killed woodcock in New Brunswick might take their birds home with them. We were obliged to point out to him, when he referred the matter to us, that sections 5 and 6 of the Export Act prohibit all export of woodcock from Canada. In consequence, these tourists who came in for the particular purpose of shooting this kind of game in Canada found that the game which they had legally shot they were prohibited from taking home with them. Provincial authorities have found themselves in a similar position in that game legally shot in one province could not be taken into another province, but they now have provincial acts whereby under permit a person may legally shoot game and legally take it out of the province to his home.
The whole purpose of this bill is to eliminate sections 5 and 6 of the Export Act. The whole matter has been before the dominion wildlife officials, who have pointed out the difficulty, and they say that the Export Game Act now covers- all that is required and that sections 5 anl 6 of the Export Act are therefore redundant and operate as a hardship against visiting tourists and sportsmen who may wish to take the game they shoot out of the country.

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of bill No. 61. to amend the Yukon Quartz Mining Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Persons who may enter and locate and lands subject to entry and location.

maintopic: CLAIM STAKING PRIVILEGES-GROUPING OF CLAIMS -NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL
speechtext: Will the minister make a statement on this section?

maintopic: CLAIM STAKING PRIVILEGES-GROUPING OF CLAIMS -NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL
speechtext:
This bill has been submitted at the request of those who have been dealing with mining in the Yukon. It has been the subject of a good deal of discussion, and I am glad to say that I have had the privilege of having the hon. member for Yukon deal with this matter, because he knows more about these matters than, probably any other person in the house. He has made representations to me coming from the miners of Yukon and from those who are interested in mining, that it is necessary that this should be done in order to protect as far as possible the rights of miners who are now going in.
In consequence of the activities which are now taking place in Yukon and elsewhere, it was felt that the provisions of this bill would
render to those miners who are going in prospecting and endeavouring to locate claims a protection of their operations. The idea of the bill is this. Formerly under this act one could only have the right to have mineral claims to a certain number. These may now be increased in number and the owners of these properties will have the right to consolidate their claims. For instance, subsection 2 and 3 provide:
(2)	Subject to section forty-five of this act during any period of twelve months no person shall be entitled to locate, whether personally, as attorney for another or by an attorney, more [DOT] than seven mineral claims in the aggregate within a distance of ten miles from any other mineral claim (making a total of eight mineral claims) located by him personally, as attorney or by attorney, during that period.
(3)	Every power of attorney authorizing a person to enter, locate, prospect or mine pursuant to subsection one of this section shall be filed with the mining recorder before the entering. locating, prospecting or mining is undertaken.
The idea is that where formerly a man made a claim he could stake only three claims within twenty days. In the meantime, when he had located the claims and had induced other prospectors to come in there, they might file adjoining claims, with the consequence that he might be deprived of all the effort and expense to which he had been put in making the original discovery. The bill gives him the right to have eight claims registered in his own name, by himself or by attorney. The matter has been carefully considered, and the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) has been extremely helpful in conveying the wishes of the people in the north with regard to the staking of claims. I am satisfied that this is a proper provision to be made for the benefit of all parties concerned.

maintopic: CLAIM STAKING PRIVILEGES-GROUPING OF CLAIMS -NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL
speechtext:
I may add a word or two to what the minister has said. The Yukon Quartz Mining Act is the legislation under which lode or hard-rock mining is done in Yukon. The act was first passed as it is now, with one slight amendment, as chapter 74 of the acts of parliament of 1924. I was member for Yukon at that time, and after consulting with the miners of Yukon I drafted an act, submitted it to the then Minister of the Interior, the Hon. Charles Stewart, in whose department Yukon was administered, who in turn submitted it to his law officers. The act was drawn, submitted to the house and then to a special committee, was finally adopted, and has been the law in Yukon since 1924. It has proved very satisfactory; but as mining is developed up there, changing to some extent from mining of placer gold to lode gold mining, it has been found that certain amendments are required and they have been clearly explained by the minister.
Placer Mining

The main object of the bill is to allow the prospector or miner to stake a group of eight claims. As the law now stands, he can stake only one in his own name and two under powers of attorney, and these powers of attorney must be accompanied by sworn evidence that the persons giving the powers of attorney have made it possible for that miner to go on that trip. Had it not been that the mining recorders and officials of Yukon had interpreted that clause generously, few claims would have been staked under it. This will eliminate any difficulties in that respect, inasmuch as it will allow a man to stake a group of claims sufficiently large to attract capital to its development. The other sections are equally important and will be dealt with section by section, I expect, in the committee. On some of these I may have something to say.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 7 inclusive agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speechtext: Subsection 4 provides that where any peace officer has reason to suspect that any person has committed or is about to commit an offence described in section 83 he may without warrant search him or any of his belongings. Surely that is giving a large amount of power to a police officer. If he suspects that a man is about to commit an offence he can search him or his belongings without a search warrant. Is there any strong justification for retaining that section, particularly this part of it which states that he is about to commit an offence?

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: One must take into consideration the place where these offences are likely to be committed. A good deal would depend on the observation of an officer who sees something which he knows is contrary to the usual practice. If he does not have that power in order to make the search, then I am afraid that he would lose the opportunity quickly if he did not act immediately and expeditiously in doing it. I do not think there is anything unusual in such a section. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are anxious that it should go in.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member for Calgary East. I do not think this parliament should ever pass sections like subsection 4 except in narcotic cases. It seems to me that we have to permit such highhanded procedure by police officers in such matters. My suggestion to the minister is that he should eliminate section 4. He should increase his penalties in subsection 1. In other words, let us have a strong deterrent, but let us not extend the position which existed in legislation during war time. Of necessity that kind of legislation exists in war time. But let us not permit a mounted policeman or any other peace officer the right to go-without penalty against him-and search people's belongings, clothing and houses. The penalty provided in subsection 1 is a term not exceed-

Placer Mining
ing three months' imprisonment and fine of $250. My thought is that if you made that a fine of $1,000 minimum and a period in gaol of three years, and in default-that is optional with the court-of payment of the fine imprisonment for at least two years you will accomplish everything you are seeking to accomplish here; in fact you will accomplish it much better than you will in this way.
In his explanatory notes the minister has said that these things are necessary because there are now more ways of leaving Yukon than there were in the old days. I appreciate that; but we shall never have enough mounted policemen in Yukon, having regard to the different and new methods of travel, to search everybody who comes out. What happens? I gather that this is high-grading. An organization which is mining finds that it is short of some raw gold. They can fairly well confine that, having regard to the circumstances, and they usually give the police a lead. Warrants are now to be found in Yukon much more easily than in the old days. There are more places where you can find them than you could heretofore. My serious suggestion to the minister is that he should increase his penalties. I do not think they are nearly large enough, having regard to the conditions under which mines operate in that country. He should increase the penalties to the point of severity, but he should eliminate adding one more place where a peace officer, even though he be a mounted policeman, can search a person, his boat, his motor car, his aeroplane, his home or even his clothing, and even his friends; I imagine they are covered. The peace officer may even take that kind of action without a warrant.
A warrant can be obtained only on the ground that some person pledges his oath that he has reason to believe that an offence has been or is going to be committed. If the magistrate so wishes he may put that person on oath and ask him the grounds for his belief. That is normal, ordinary procedure. With great respect I am going to suggest to the minister that he reconsider this section.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext:
I quite agree with the hon. member for Calgary West, and with all due respect to the minister, that the penalties provided by section 83A should be increased. As I see it, a fine not exceeding $250 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months or a sentence to both such fine and such imprisonment is altogether too light to create any fear in wrongdoers, thieves or high-graders.
I must say that I do not agree with the hon. member for Calgary West or with others who object to subsection 4 because, having lived all my life in Yukon and having seen
the Royal Canadian Mounted Police up there, I know that no innocent person will be inconvenienced by them, and the baggage of no one will be searched unless the police have good reason to suspect that it has high-grade gold or stolen material in it. So far as I am concerned I should like to see the subsection stand as it is drafted, but I would suggest to the minister that the penalty for high-grading or theft of gold or export of gold without a proper permit should be increased.
Mr. HAZEN; I cannot sit in this committee and allow this section to pass without taking objection to it. It is a principle of our law that every person who is accused of an offence is presumed innocent until proved guilty. Under this section a person does not have to be accused of an offence before the mounted police can, if they suspect that he is about to commit an offence, proceed against him.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: No; they may search him.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext:
Yes, proceed against him and search him. The section reads:
Where any peace officer has reason to suspect that any person has committed or is about to commit an offence . . .
A peace officer is no wiser than any other person. How he can form a judgment as to whether or not a person is about to commit an offence, or suspects that a person is about to commit an offence, is more than I can understand. Legislation of this kind should not be passed by this committee.
The minister said that we must take into consideration the place where the offence is committed. Well, this place is Yukon territory. In Yukon territory there are places like Dawson city, which is a town of some size, where there are police officers and where I suppose there is a form of municipal government. Why should the police of Dawson city be permitted, because they suspect a person is about to commit an offence, to take any action against that person under the principles of the law under which we live in this country? As I say, I cannot let this section pass without protesting against it. It should be eliminated from the bill.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: How does this section compare with similar sections in provincial acts?

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext:
In this matter we are dealing not with the question of high-grading but with the question of royalties which should be paid. As I said before, conditions are such that any person leaving would be doing so with such expedition that the officer would be unable to obtain a warrant in time to
Placer Mining

seize the gold and exact the royalty due upon it. I agree with the hon. member for Yukon that subsection 4 should be retained. I have no doubt that any officer dealing with these matters, having some idea and knowledge of what rvas happening, would have direct evidence in his own mind that such a thing was being done; and if he did not take action immediately he would not be able to catch the person he suspected. As far as the penalty is concerned there seems to be a disposition to regard it as too lenient. The hon. member for Calgary West suggests a rather extreme penalty of $1,000 and a term not exceeding three years, or to both such fine and imprisonment. I would be willing to have an amendment moved to that effect, provided that upon summary conviction a person would be liable to a fine of not more than $1,000, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or to both suo'h fine and imprisonment, if my colleague would move it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: I move accordingly.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: Will that amendment be to paragraph (f) of section 1?

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: That is in section 2 of the bill, subsection 1; the words "two hundred and fifty" in line 22 to be deleted and the words "one thousand" substituted therefor; and in lines 24 and 25 the words "three months" to be deleted and the words "three 3Tears" to be substituted therefor.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: The committee has heard the amendment read by the minister. Shall section 2 carry as amended?

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: No. I should like to ask the minister this question. Is the export of gold without paying a royalty a tremendously serious offence? Is it any more serious than many of the offences which are now dealt with in our criminal code and for which the penalty is very much less? How do this offence and this penalty compare with many of the provisions in the criminal code having to do with the same matters?

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext:
With all due respect to the hon. member for St. John-Albert, I think the criminal code would be improved by making those penalties much more stringent than they are now. They are too light. They do not create any fear on the part of criminals. Even with the proposed amendment, increasing the maximum fine to $1,000, a convicting magistrate or judge may make the fine not more than $10 if he wishes, depending upon the circumstances of the case. Because

we say "not to exceed one thousand dollars," that does not mean in every case the person convicted will be fined that amount, or that he will be imprisoned for three years. He may get only three months, within the judgment of the convicting magistrate or judge.
As to its being a crime to take gold out of Yukon without paying the royalty, in old times when gold was exported almost entirely in its natural state, that is in the form of gold dust or nuggets, it was very easy to steal gold. At that time the mounted police had not only male searchers but female searchers to search women passengers. Before a person was allowed to leave Yukon he or she was searched for gold, if they had any reason to suspect that he or she would be taking out that gold. "Even within the past two years gold was stolen in its natural state from one of the big dredging machines up there. They noticed that a theft had been committed, and also that a couple of members of the crew had quit within a short time. So the police met these men at the airport when they were about to board a plane and made them open up their grips; and there was the gold dust. They did not wait for a warrant to do that; if they had done so the men would have been out of the territory and into the United States. I think the subsection should remain just as it is. To-day the great bulk of gold shipped from Yukon goes through the banks and is sent out in gold bricks, of a value not less than $10,000 each. It is almost impossible to steal those; they are too bulky and thieves cannot get away with them. But in the natural form of gold dust and nuggets it is easy enough to steal and conceal, so that I think the penalty should be severe, and I belive the police officers should be given a free hand to discover and search any thieves.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext:
I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Yukon. It is important that we realize that laws which are necessary for a city like Calgary or Saint John are not applicable to these northern areas. We must recognize that one who seeks to evade his responsibility in the payment of royalties is trying to cheat his fellow citizens, and all this section asks is:
Where any police officer has reason to suspect that any person has committed or is about to commit an offence ... or has in his possession or in his belongings any gold in respect of which the royalty . . . has not been paid, such police officer may without warrant search such person and his belongings. . . .
If that provision is not made, as the hon. member for Yukon points out, a person may be out of the country by plane within a very short time. Most of us have our baggage examined for customs purposes whenever we

Placer Mining
cross the international boundary, and we do not particularly object. If the individual has no gold that he is trying to take out of the country without paying the royalty, no serious damage will be done. So that I think the hon. member for Yukon is quite right in urging that this section should be retained in its present form.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: In listening to this debate, one would think gold is one of our most precious metals. Actually I believe it is one of the least important at this time. If we are to live up to the Bretton Woods agreement, which w'e talked about so much, we should not be so worried about gold just now. However, I rose to say that I am opposed to any increase in the penalty in subsection 2; and as far as that is concerned I am entirely opposed to subsection 4. After all, we are dealing with human beings, whether they are in gold mining areas or anywhere else, and here we are giving police officers the right to go through a person's belongings. It will be noted that in the second last line it says, "and any articles believed to be bis belongings." They do not even have to know for sure that the belongings are those of the person they are searching; they may search the belongings of other people. I believe this is placing too much power in the hands of the police, and I want to record my objection to both subsections.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: I wonder if we could get together on this. I have a suggestion to make with respect to subsection 4.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: I wonder if we could clear up section 2. Shall subsection 1, of section 2 carry as amended? Then we can go on.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: Do you not think they are definitely related, sir?

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: Go ahead.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext:
No; they have
nothing to do with each other.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext:
My hon.
friend says they have nothing to do with each other, but surely what we are trying to do here is to prevent crime or, once we find it, to punish it. The deterrents which I suggested to the minister, and which he adopted, in exacting greater penalties under subsection 2, were as a deterrent to the crime itself.
With respect to subsection 4, we find .the words:
Where any peace officer has reason to suspect that any person has committed or is about to commit an offence . . .
I wonder if we cannot arrive somewhere by adding the word "sufficient" before the word "reason", and then eliminating the- words "or is about to commit". I have had occasion to say before in the house that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are a very fine force of men. But we all know that you cannot have four or five thousand men-and I think their . numbers must be about that by this time- and have them all saints. It seems to me the wishes of the minister would be met by adding the word "sufficient". He would meet those cases where it is suggested that someone has heard a person has done something and escaped by aeroplane. Then such a person may have been picked up at the end of his journey, a search made, and the person taken from the aeroplane. In that instance the officer would have sufficient reason for believing that an offence had been committed.
In connection with a failure to pay royalties on gold, how can it be said that we suspect a person is about to commit an offence? The offence is the removal of gold from Yukon territory.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: Not necessarily; in most instances it is stolen gold.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: High-grading, if you like.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: No, not highgrading.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: With great respect to the hon. member for Yukon may I say that this does not deal with theft; rather it is a matter of failing to pay royalties. I am accepting the minister's word for that, because that is what he said only a minute ago. How can it be said a person is about to remove gold? If that is all, how can a [DOT] search help? If a man has gold in his pocket or his pouch-and perhaps the hon. member for Yukon is thinking of that night on the marge of lake Labarge they cremated Sam McGee-

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: That is just rubbish.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: But delightful rubbish, by the way.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: And you do not entertain the committee with it, one bit.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: It would assist an officer in finding someone who is about to commit an offence.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext:
With all due respect,
I cannot see why members should be so filled with fear that some crook is going to be inconvenienced-and that is all it means. If a person has not stolen gold, or has not gold
Placer Mining

on his body or on his person, he will not be inconvenienced by the officers. One hon. member mentioned that when one crosses the boundary the customs officers search the baggage. I have seen them search their persons. The suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary West would make it even more drastic than it is now. I am all for subsection 4 as it is.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext: I suggest to the minister that the words "or is about to commit" be deleted. The hon. member for Yukon has referred to the searching of baggage by customs officers, but I would point out that that is a different matter altogether. They lay open the bags and take a cursory look, but that is a different matter altogether from permitting police officers to have power to search one's person or belongings, simply because there has been a suspicion that someone may be going to commit an offence. It is bad enough to give power to a police officer to make a search when he has good reason to suspect that an offence has been committed. This section will allow such officers to search anyone at any time in Yukon.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext:
The words in the section are:
Where any peace officer has reason to suspect that any person has committed or is about to commit an offence.
He does not commit the offence until he is actually outside the territory and evading the payment of royalty. If we eliminate from the section the words "or is about to commit" we take the teeth from it. What would happen would be that a peace officer would know about a man who is about to commit an offence, namely, of his intention to leave the territory in a hurry, by aeroplane, train or team-

speechtext: Or boat.

subtopic: NON-FORFEITURE OF CLAIMS OF SERVICE PERSONNEL-SMUGGLING
speechtext:
Unless the man is searched at that time, the man will have left the territory; the offence will have been committed and the officer left in a position where he could do nothing. If those words were taken out the section would not be effective.

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and
Resources) moved the second reading of bill No. 63, respecting the boundaries of certain national parks.

He said: Mr. Speaker, as this bill, if enacted, will divest the crown of certain areas of land in certain national parks, title to which is at present in the crown. The governor general has been informed in respect thereto, and has given his consent to consideration of the bill.

subtopic: ADJUSTMENT OF BOUNDARIES IN RESPECT OF CERTAIN SMALL AREAS
speechtext: Should that not have been done before? Is this the proper time to indicate the assent of the crown to this legislation?

subtopic: ADJUSTMENT OF BOUNDARIES IN RESPECT OF CERTAIN SMALL AREAS

subtopic: ADJUSTMENT OF BOUNDARIES IN RESPECT OF CERTAIN SMALL AREAS
speechtext: With great deference to the minister I should think it is a strange procedure if the parliament of Canada can get as far as second reading before obtaining the consent of the governor general, and acquainting the house with that fact. I think something must be wrong, somewhere. It is certainly new to me; I never heard of this procedure before.

subtopic: ADJUSTMENT OF BOUNDARIES IN RESPECT OF CERTAIN SMALL AREAS
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Peel has in mind a resolution involving a payment of money, in respect of which it should be indicated that His Excellency the Governor General has given consent. But that is not this case. This is not dealing with a question of money but divesting the crown of parts of areas in the parks, and I am instructed by the law officers that that statement should be made before the motion is put.

subtopic: ADJUSTMENT OF BOUNDARIES IN RESPECT OF CERTAIN SMALL AREAS
speechtext:
I should explain to the committee that although Banff park is described by metes and bounds in the National Parks Act, the boundaries of Banff park were not surveyed until 1940 when on instructions from the surveyor general a survey was made and boundary posts set up. Following the survey, an official map of the park was prepared.
This map was approved and signed on behalf of the Dominion of Canada by the Hon. T. A. Crerar, Minister of Mines and Resources, under authority of an order of His Excellency the Governor in Council and on behalf of the province of Alberta by the Hon. N. E. Tanner, Minister of Lands and Mines. An original signed copy of the said map was filed in the land titles office for the South Alberta land registration district of Calgary on the 18th April, 1941.

National Parks
Two small parcels of land not formerly in the park are included within the boundaries of the park, as set out in schedule A. One parcel containing approximately 210 acres was acquired as a site for the eastern gateway. The other parcel comprising one-sixth square mile due to an adjustment of the boundary made on the survey of the park is added with the approval of the province. Total area added is approximately one-half square mile.
The total area of the park as described in schedule A is 2,585 square miles more or less.
Then as to Kootenay Park, the original agreement known as the Banff-Windermere road agreement which was approved by the dominion government by orders in council dated the 14th and 20th March, 1919, and ratified by an Act of the provincial legislature known as the Banff-Windermere Road Agreement Ratification Act, being chapter 5, British Columbia statutes, 1919, contained the following provision:
(4) The said province will grant to the dominion government a strip of land along the said Banff-Windermere road as laid out and completed to an approximate width of five (5) miles on each side thereof; provided always that, as far as possible, the crests of the mountains shall constitute the outside boundaries of the said area.
Kootenay park as established by order in council, P.C. 827, in 1920 included the area granted by the province of British Columbia.
A small part of the park unsuitable for park purposes was removed from the park area by order in council, P.C. 209, of February 2, 1922, following an arrangement with the province.
An official survey of and map showing the boundaries of Kootenay park were made under instructions from the surveyor general.
Upon completion of the survey, it was found that the park area varied considerably from the area mentioned in the original agreement, but the principle set out in the proviso of section 4 of that agreement was maintained in that the survey fixed the boundaries of the park along the crest of the mountains.
The provincial government of British Columbia, upon the completion of the survey and map, implemented the above-mentioned statute, chapter 5, British Columbia statutes, 1919, by passing order in council No. 810 of August 8, 1928, approving of the survey and the boundaries fixed by the survey. The boundaries of Kootenay park, as surveyed, are set out in schedule A to the bill.
The area of the park when established in 1920 was estimated at 587 square miles. Approximately seven square miles were removed from the park in 1922. Upon completion of the survey, the area of the park was established as 543 square miles, more or less.
Next is Riding Mountain park. The department acquired a number of small areas comprising in all slightly less than two sections with some pieces of roadway as an addition to the Riding Mountain park. These areas lie immediately south of the townsite of Wasagaming, the headquarters of the park. They were specially required to round out the park in this important section. The area being added consists of 962.3 acres.
This is similar to what was done in connection with Banff park. They had to add a portion of land at the south gateway in order to protect the entrance and prevent the building of hotels and the erection of other buildings at the gateway of the park.
The two small areas being withdrawn from the park were former sites of the forest officer's headquarters when the park area was a forest reserve. These two areas are outside the .main park area.
Upon the establishment of the park a more intensive administration of the area was organized under which it was found advisable to locate the park wardens inside the park. The improvements upon these two small areas have been disposed of and the said areas are not now being used as they are in the centre of a farming district. It is considered they should be available for agricultural purposes. The total area of the two parcels being withdrawn is 320 acres.
The total area of the park is approximately 1,148 square miles.
Then Point Pelee park. The areas being added to Point Pelee park comprise:
(a)	Part of a number of squatters' holdings which the department purchased from the estate of Joseph W. Post, together with some adjoining lands, the title to which was in the crown in the right of the dominion but which were not included in the park;
(b)	Two lots in a subdivision of lot one of the squatters' holdings which the department acquired at a tax sale;
(c)	With the formal consent of the local municipality. the department expropriated the roads inside the park boundaries.
The total area of the parcels being added to the park consists of 255-03 acres. The total area of the park is 3,869 acres, including the additions.
I come next to Georgian bay islands parks. Flowerpot island, which it is desired to include in the Georgian bay islands park, is located at the head of the Bruce peninsula.
The island was surrendered by the Chippewa Indians on the 5th day of June, 1856, and was acquired for park purposes from the Department of Indian Affairs on the 6th December, 1930.
National Parks

With the addition of Flowerpot island, Georgian bay islands parks will consist of Beausoleil island (2,712 acres), Flowerpot island (475 acres) and some 28 smaller islands (251 acres), a total area of approximately 3,438 acres.
Mr. MaoNICOL: Have squatters any rights there now?

speechtext: No.

The next is Mallorytown landing park. The new scenic highway which the provincial government is constructing between Brock-ville and Gananoque runs through the Mallorytown landing park, one of the St. Lawrence Islands parks. The idea of this whole bill is to round out, under the surveys that have been made, the boundaries of the parks, including some portions and excluding other portions.
